book_title: Chapter 3: Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
question: How does a ₹100 invoice travel through AXISCADES' cost structure—and why did ₹72 crore of FY26 accounting profit turn into -₹1 crore of operating cash flow?

epigraph.quote: Revenue is vanity, EBITDA is opinion, and working capital is the truth—especially when your customer is a defence ministry or a public-sector prime.
epigraph.author: Forensic Cash-Flow Principle

web_blocks.title: Go-to-Market Architecture: Direct OEM Key Accounts vs. Indian Defence Procurement

web_blocks.html: AXISCADES does not sell through retail dealers, distributors, or online stores. Its sales engine is a dual-track B2B and B2G model [1][2]. In global Aerospace and ESAI, sales flow through multi-year Master Service Agreements (MSAs) and Statement-of-Work (SoW) hubs near Tier-1 OEM clusters. These include Airbus in Toulouse and Hamburg, Boeing and chip leaders in North America, and R&D centers in Bengaluru [2][3]. Winning an OEM vendor code takes 18–36 months of AS9100 quality, export-control, and cyber audits. Once embedded in a jet or chip program, switching costs are high, and billing is monthly or milestone-based on clean corporate credit terms.

In Indian Defence, however, sales follow the Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP), DRDO Transfer-of-Technology (ToT) rules, and Bharat Electronics, HAL, or Indian Army tenders [4][5]. Instead of smooth monthly billing, defence hardware follows a lumpier path: prototype design, User Evaluation Trials (UET) in harsh terrain, batch orders, Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT), and milestone-gated payments [4][6]. Moving from monthly service billing to milestone-gated hardware explains both higher gross margins and wider working-capital swings.

web_blocks.title: Supply Chain & Manufacturing Footprint: Devanahalli (DAC) & Hyderabad (MAC)

web_blocks.html: As AXISCADES shifts from services to serial production under Power 930, its supply chain is changing too. It now relies less on hiring engineers and more on buying mil-spec FPGAs, ASICs, liquid-cooled boxes, and precision parts [4][7]. In Q4 FY26, part shortages in defence land systems forced AXISCADES to defer ₹142 crore of sales into FY27. That delay proved hardware output is vulnerable to long-lead military chip and sub-vendor bottlenecks [4]. To bring assembly and testing in-house, the firm is building the Devanahalli Atmanirbhar Complex (DAC / Aeroland) in Bengaluru and the Missile Atmanirbhar Complex (MAC) in Hyderabad. As a result, Fixed Assets jumped from ₹398 crore in Mar 2025 to ₹459 crore in Mar 2026 and ₹698 crore by Sep 2026 [8][9].

web_blocks.title: FY2026 Unit Economics Waterfall: From ₹1,159 Crore Revenue to -₹1 Crore Operating Cash

web_blocks.html: The waterfall below breaks down AXISCADES' audited FY2026 consolidated P&L and cash flow [8]. Every ₹100 of FY26 sales (₹1,159 crore total) spent ₹47.80 on staff costs (₹554 crore total: ₹503.29 crore in Technology Services and ₹51.11 crore in Defence) [8][10]. Another ₹36.84 covered materials, subcontracting, and other overheads (₹427 crore total: ~₹225 crore direct COGS and ~₹202 crore other opex). That left ₹15.36 in operating EBITDA (₹178 crore) [8]. Deducting ₹3.80 for depreciation (₹44 crore) and ₹2.76 for interest (₹32 crore), and adding ₹1.04 of other income (₹12 crore), gave ₹9.84 in pre-tax profit (₹114 crore). After a 37% effective tax rate, net profit came to ₹6.21 per ₹100 (₹72 crore) [8].

web_blocks.caption: FY2026 Consolidated Unit Economics & Cash Conversion Waterfall (INR Crore)
web_blocks.takeaway: While FY26 operating EBITDA expanded 24% YoY to ₹178 Cr (15.4% OPM) and PAT reached ₹72 Cr, working-capital absorption (130 debtor days, ₹411 Cr receivables) dragged CFO to -₹1 Cr and FCF to -₹135 Cr.

web_blocks.html: Here lies the core forensic lesson of Chapter 3. While AXISCADES earned ₹72 crore in FY26 net profit, Cash Flow from Operations (CFO) fell to -₹1 crore (down from ₹88 crore in FY25). After ₹134 crore of capex, Free Cash Flow (FCF) plunged to -₹135 crore [8]. Why did ₹178 crore of EBITDA turn into negative cash? First, trade receivables swelled to ₹411 crore, pushing Debtor Days from 89 (FY24) to 107 (FY25) and 130 days (FY26) [8][11]. Second, inventory and WIP built up ahead of delayed land-system deliveries, lifting Inventory Days from 104 to 121 [8]. Days Payable also jumped from 100 to 220 days as the firm leaned on vendor credit to offset slow collections—a temporary buffer that will eventually unwind.

web_blocks.caption: Working Capital & Cash Conversion Trajectory (FY22–FY26)
web_blocks.takeaway: A 41-day surge in Debtor Days between FY24 and FY26—combined with heavy capex for Devanahalli and defence lines—temporarily broke AXISCADES' cash conversion, forcing reliance on short-term project borrowings.

web_blocks.title: Post-Akkodis Unit Economics: How the Cost Structure Resets in FY27–FY28

web_blocks.html: Once Phase 1 and Phase 2 of the Akkodis deal finish, AXISCADES' cost mix will shift sharply. Staff costs—which took 47.8% of FY26 sales due to thousands of billable ER&D engineers—will drop as a share of revenue. At the same time, direct parts (FPGAs, RF chips, rugged boxes) and depreciation (DAC and MAC equipment) will rise. This is the classic shift from a people-led services P&L to a hardware-led factory P&L. High factory utilization drives strong operating leverage, yet fixed-asset intensity and working capital suffer fast if client sign-offs slip.

web_blocks.title: The Project-Debt & Cost-of-Capital Reality
paragraphs: To bridge slow defence receivables and higher inventory, AXISCADES raised gross borrowings (at ~9.5% working-capital rates and ~8%–8.5% AIF rates) from ₹258 crore in Mar 2025 to ₹388 crore in Mar 2026 and ₹698 crore by Sep 2026 [8][12]. Post-Akkodis proceeds (~₹2,256 crore across tranches) are meant to retire this bridge debt and fund capex without lasting leverage. Receiving those tranches on time and cutting DSO back under 90 days is the single biggest unit-economic test for FY27–FY28.

web_blocks.title: Supplier Concentration, Import Dependencies & Margin Sensitivity

web_blocks.html: A final cost lever is part sourcing. Mistral designs its own signal boards and firmware in Bengaluru, but top-end FPGAs, rad-hard memory, and RF parts still come from global mil-spec distributors. When lead times stretch or export permits slow—as in the ₹142 crore Q4 FY26 land-system delay [4]—AXISCADES must hold extra buffer stock (121 inventory days in FY26) to protect schedules. In-house assembly at Devanahalli (DAC) and Hyderabad (MAC) captures testing margins, yet it cannot remove chip lead-time risk. Investors should therefore model steady-state continuing EBITDA margins at 16%–20% rather than straight-line gains.

web_blocks.title: Capital Intensity & Asset Turns: The Shift from Services to Manufacturing

web_blocks.html: When AXISCADES was mostly an ER&D services firm, growth needed very little capex. From FY19 to FY22, investing cash outlays stayed small, and Free Cash Flow stayed positive (₹30 Cr, ₹59 Cr, ₹117 Cr, and ₹18 Cr) [8]. By contrast, building Devanahalli (DAC) and the Hyderabad Missile Complex (MAC) pushed FY26 capex to ₹134 crore (11.6% of sales) and lifted Fixed Assets plus CWIP from ₹406 crore (Mar 2025) to ₹734 crore (Sep 2026) [8]. To compound returns, those new plants must earn at least 2.0x–2.5x asset turns on new fixed capital. Otherwise, higher depreciation (₹44 crore in FY26, ₹42 crore TTM) will hold down Return on Capital Employed (ROCE).

In short, AXISCADES' unit economics sit at a classic factory inflection. Gross and operating margins are rising as hourly services give way to defence electronics and aero hardware. Still, cash conversion will stay tied to 130-day receivables and heavy capex until Devanahalli hits full utilization and Akkodis cash pays down bridge debt.

book_paragraphs: To see if an engineering firm is truly compounding or just running in place, ignore the press releases. Instead, trace one ₹100 invoice from the client's desk to the bank account. In AXISCADES, that journey moves at two very different speeds. On the global aerospace and chip side, you sign a Master Service Agreement with Airbus, Boeing, or a chipmaker, staff engineers in Bengaluru or Europe, and bill monthly. Collections are steady. On the Indian defence side, you deal with DRDO labs, Bharat Electronics, and the Ministry of Defence. Contracts are milestone-gated, Factory Acceptance Testing takes months, and one missing overseas part can freeze a ₹142 crore shipment—just as happened in Q4 FY26. Understanding that two-speed cash cycle is essential before reading any quarterly profit figure.

Let us walk through the FY2026 consolidated waterfall together. Out of ₹1,159 crore in sales—picture it as ₹100 on the top line—₹47.80 paid employee salaries and benefits (₹554 crore across technology services and defence). Another ₹36.84 covered materials, subcontracting, and operating overheads (₹427 crore combined). That left a solid ₹15.36 in operating EBITDA, or ₹178 crore—up nearly 25% year-on-year. After deducting ₹3.80 for depreciation and ₹2.76 for interest, adding ₹1.04 in other income, and paying taxes, AXISCADES reported ₹6.21 of net profit per ₹100 of sales, or ₹72 crore total.

Now here is the forensic punchline that separates careful analysts from casual readers. Out of that ₹72 crore in net profit and ₹178 crore in EBITDA, how much operating cash actually hit the bank in FY26? Minus ₹1 crore. And once you subtract ₹134 crore of capex for sites like the Devanahalli Atmanirbhar Complex and the Hyderabad Missile Complex, Free Cash Flow was minus ₹135 crore. That ₹135 crore cash outflow explains why debt rose sharply even in a profitable year.

Why did the cash vanish? Look at the working-capital dials. Debtor days climbed from 80 days in FY23 to 89 in FY24, 107 in FY25, and 130 days in FY26, locking up ₹411 crore in unpaid bills. Inventory days rose to 121 days as parts sat on the floor waiting for delayed land-system shipments. Meanwhile, days payable stretched to 220 days as the firm leaned on vendor credit. To fund operations and build Devanahalli, borrowings jumped from ₹258 crore in March 2025 to ₹388 crore in March 2026 and ₹698 crore by September 2026, at working-capital interest rates near 9.5%. In short, working capital absorbed more cash than the entire year's operating profit generated.

As the Akkodis sale closes, the cost structure itself will change. Staff costs will fall as a share of sales once legacy staffing exits, while material costs and depreciation rise. Swapping linear wage inflation for factory operating leverage only works if inventory turns fast and defence bills clear inside 90 days. That is why the Akkodis deal is not just a portfolio cleanup—it is a balance-sheet rescue valve. If the sale cash lands on time and DSO drops back toward 80 to 90 days as deferred shipments clear, free cash flow will snap back into positive territory. Until that cash sits in the bank, working capital stays our top watch item.

book_subsections.title: The Hidden Cost of Milestone Delays
paragraphs: When a services firm misses a quarterly goal, it simply delays billing hours. When a hardware integrator misses a milestone because one vendor delays a rugged connector, millions of rupees of paid parts sit idle on the floor while 9.5% interest ticks every day. That asymmetry is the core operational risk of moving from 3% design to 97% manufacturing.

Look closely at vendor credit in FY26 as well: Days Payable jumped from 100 days in FY25 to 220 days in FY26. AXISCADES partly cushioned its 130-day receivable stretch by paying its own suppliers slower. You can pull that lever once during a tight quarter, but you cannot stretch vendors to 220 days forever without risking part allocations or losing cash discounts.

book_subsections.title: What Clean Unit Economics Should Look Like by FY28
paragraphs: What does success look like on the unit-economic dashboard over the next two years? First, as Akkodis Phase 1 and Phase 2 proceeds arrive, gross debt should fall sharply from the ₹698 crore September 2026 peak. That will cut quarterly interest costs from ₹9–₹12 crore toward low single digits. Second, once the deferred ₹142 crore land-system orders pass Factory Acceptance Testing and DRDO/BEL billing normalizes, Debtor Days must drop from 130 days back into the 80-to-90-day band. Third, as Devanahalli and Hyderabad scale up, operating cash flow should recover to 65%–75% of pre-tax EBITDA, matching the 78% rate hit in FY24 and FY25.

Also watch fixed-asset turnover closely. Spending ₹134 crore on capex in FY26 and lifting Fixed Assets plus CWIP to ₹734 crore by September 2026 created a fixed commitment. Depreciation will stay near ₹40 to ₹50 crore a year whether the plants run full or half-empty. Those plants must generate at least two rupees of annual sales per rupee of net fixed assets to push ROCE above 15%. Until debt falls, DSO normalizes, and Devanahalli ships serial batches, we treat the FY26 waterfall as a yellow light.

book_callouts.title: Never Confuse Deferred Revenue with Collected Cash
book_callouts.text: Management rightly noted that ₹142 crore of Q4 FY26 defence sales was deferred, not cancelled. Still, every extra month an order sits in WIP or receivables costs roughly 9.5% annualized working-capital interest.
